Pearson/logistic relations describe observed helpfulness associations.

source.title: Sales Strategy Recommendation Based on Commodity Data Mining

source_quality.summary: All 43 pages were read and visually reconciled. The source contains Summary, Introduction, cleaning/NLTK sentiment, Pearson/logistic relations, LDA aspects, similarity/AHP scores, brand clustering, AR(1)/seasonality, Almon lags, sensitivity, assessment, a team letter, appendix tables and code.

decisions: which product attributes require improvement, which brands form a candidate group, when reputation peaks may support sales activity, how prior rating/review histories relate to current reviews, and how managers should monitor customer feedback

title: Sales Strategy Recommendation Based on Commodity Data Mining
unresolved_questions: The source PDF is a paper-internal recommendation, not the official problem statement.
The Summary's four questions are scope, not measured outcomes.
Data reliability is assumed before it is audited.
Duplicate and missing-value rules lack a row-level deletion ledger.
The concrete redundant-review example motivates similarity filtering but does not prove fraud.
NLTK compound sentiment is bounded but not independently accuracy-tested.
Tokenization and lowercasing can alter sentiment features.
Emoji, sarcasm and context can escape the lexicon.
A positive word in a negative phrase can mislead a dictionary score.
Review length and helpfulness can be exposure-dependent.
Pearson correlation is not causal identification.
Multinomial logistic coefficients depend on class coding and reference class.
Squared terms can create a U-shape only over the observed data range.
Logistic fit quality and residual diagnostics are incompletely reported.
LDA topic labels are human interpretations of word distributions.
Topic number and initialization can change the five-aspect map.
Similarity scores inherit the selected aspect vocabulary.
Star rating plus text scores do not automatically form a validated construct.
AHP pairwise judgments are subjective even when the consistency ratio passes.
AHP weights are not calibrated against sales or margin.
Brand ranks are sample- and product-specific.
System-cluster labels depend on distance, scaling and cut level.
Cluster stability across seeds is not shown.
High-quality cluster membership is not proof of future sales success.
AR(1) order from ACF/PACF is a diagnostic choice, not a guarantee.
AIC/BIC favor parsimony but do not replace a chronological holdout.
White-noise residual assumptions are not fully demonstrated.
Monthly aggregation loses daily exposure and launch detail.
Seasonal peaks may reflect omitted holidays or catalog changes.
Reputation forecasts lack intervals and rolling-origin error.
Short forecast horizons should not be read as long-run guarantees.
The 70/30 emotional/star reputation weight is author-selected.
The page-20 sensitivity percentages must be read from the raster because OCR splits small cells.
Perturbing one weight does not quantify joint uncertainty.
Distributed-lag coefficients depend on lag length and exposure definition.
Almon polynomials impose a smooth lag shape.
A lagged association is not review contagion.
Current review emotion may share unmeasured product shocks with past ratings.
Synchrony plots do not identify direction of influence.
Quality-word frequency is not engineering priority without cost and testing.
High rating and low emotion can indicate mismatch, but not false reviews by itself.
Clustered extreme words do not prove manipulation.
Appendix coefficient tables are not additional independent samples.
Printed code is not a successful rerun in the missing environment.
Hard-coded file paths limit reproducibility.
No random seed or package version is frozen for LDA/clustering.
Product heterogeneity is not fully modeled.
Reviewer selection and verified/Vine status can confound brand comparisons.
Sales, price, inventory and margin are not directly observed outcomes.
The marketing letter compresses evidence and may sound more certain than the body.
Hair-dryer efficiency advice needs engineering and safety validation.
Microwave size and after-sale advice needs cost and service-capacity checks.
Pacifier thermal and design advice needs safety testing.
Seasonal investment advice needs inventory and demand checks.
A dated recipient does not make the memo validated.
The conclusion should preserve descriptive, predictive and recommendation boundaries.
A high R-squared can coexist with poor out-of-sample performance.
A significant coefficient can be practically small.
A non-significant result should not be silently omitted.
Multiple tests can inflate false-positive risk.
No multiplicity adjustment is reported for the many comparisons.
Sensitivity values do not cover changed topic vocabularies or lag windows.
The same historical records support construction and verification of several indices.
Future data drift can change word meaning and review behavior.
Product-parent aggregation can hide brand-level variation.
Missing dates and repairs can distort seasonality.
A manager needs trigger, monitor and reversal criteria for each action.
Recommendations lack explicit decision costs and service constraints.
Model updates and retraining cadence are not specified.
The evidence chain is useful as a writing pattern only when every number retains product, horizon, denominator and claim type.

Eight bounded JPEGs were inspected one per call; original PNGs remained disk-only.

weaknesses.summary: The source PDF is a paper-internal recommendation, not the official problem statement.
The Summary's four questions are scope, not measured outcomes.
Data reliability is assumed before it is audited.
Duplicate and missing-value rules lack a row-level deletion ledger.
The concrete redundant-review example motivates similarity filtering but does not prove fraud.
NLTK compound sentiment is bounded but not independently accuracy-tested.
Tokenization and lowercasing can alter sentiment features.
Emoji, sarcasm and context can escape the lexicon.
A positive word in a negative phrase can mislead a dictionary score.
Review length and helpfulness can be exposure-dependent.
Pearson correlation is not causal identification.
Multinomial logistic coefficients depend on class coding and reference class.
Squared terms can create a U-shape only over the observed data range.
Logistic fit quality and residual diagnostics are incompletely reported.
LDA topic labels are human interpretations of word distributions.
Topic number and initialization can change the five-aspect map.
Similarity scores inherit the selected aspect vocabulary.
Star rating plus text scores do not automatically form a validated construct.
AHP pairwise judgments are subjective even when the consistency ratio passes.
AHP weights are not calibrated against sales or margin.
Brand ranks are sample- and product-specific.
System-cluster labels depend on distance, scaling and cut level.
Cluster stability across seeds is not shown.
High-quality cluster membership is not proof of future sales success.
AR(1) order from ACF/PACF is a diagnostic choice, not a guarantee.
AIC/BIC favor parsimony but do not replace a chronological holdout.
White-noise residual assumptions are not fully demonstrated.
Monthly aggregation loses daily exposure and launch detail.
Seasonal peaks may reflect omitted holidays or catalog changes.
Reputation forecasts lack intervals and rolling-origin error.
Short forecast horizons should not be read as long-run guarantees.
The 70/30 emotional/star reputation weight is author-selected.
The page-20 sensitivity percentages must be read from the raster because OCR splits small cells.
Perturbing one weight does not quantify joint uncertainty.
Distributed-lag coefficients depend on lag length and exposure definition.
Almon polynomials impose a smooth lag shape.
A lagged association is not review contagion.
Current review emotion may share unmeasured product shocks with past ratings.
Synchrony plots do not identify direction of influence.
Quality-word frequency is not engineering priority without cost and testing.
High rating and low emotion can indicate mismatch, but not false reviews by itself.
Clustered extreme words do not prove manipulation.
Appendix coefficient tables are not additional independent samples.
Printed code is not a successful rerun in the missing environment.
Hard-coded file paths limit reproducibility.
No random seed or package version is frozen for LDA/clustering.
Product heterogeneity is not fully modeled.
Reviewer selection and verified/Vine status can confound brand comparisons.
Sales, price, inventory and margin are not directly observed outcomes.
The marketing letter compresses evidence and may sound more certain than the body.
Hair-dryer efficiency advice needs engineering and safety validation.
Microwave size and after-sale advice needs cost and service-capacity checks.
Pacifier thermal and design advice needs safety testing.
Seasonal investment advice needs inventory and demand checks.
A dated recipient does not make the memo validated.
The conclusion should preserve descriptive, predictive and recommendation boundaries.
A high R-squared can coexist with poor out-of-sample performance.
A significant coefficient can be practically small.
A non-significant result should not be silently omitted.
Multiple tests can inflate false-positive risk.
No multiplicity adjustment is reported for the many comparisons.
Sensitivity values do not cover changed topic vocabularies or lag windows.
The same historical records support construction and verification of several indices.
Future data drift can change word meaning and review behavior.
Product-parent aggregation can hide brand-level variation.
Missing dates and repairs can distort seasonality.
A manager needs trigger, monitor and reversal criteria for each action.
Recommendations lack explicit decision costs and service constraints.
Model updates and retraining cadence are not specified.
The evidence chain is useful as a writing pattern only when every number retains product, horizon, denominator and claim type.
